title: America Just Declared Children's Screen Time a Public Health Crisis. Some of the Damage May Be Permanent.
excerpt: The Surgeon General set the strictest-ever federal limits on digital device use. A companion study says developmental windows missed to screens may never reopen.
body:
The United States Surgeon General has issued a new advisory classifying excessive screen time among children and adolescents as a public health crisis, establishing the strictest federal guidelines on digital device use ever issued in the country.

The advisory comes with concrete, age-specific limits: zero screen time for infants and toddlers under 18 months, less than one hour per day for children between 18 months and six years, and a maximum of two hours of digital entertainment per day for those aged six to 18.

The Department of Health and Human Services is also calling on schools to implement campus-wide bans on non-instructional phones during school hours — a practice that dozens of states have already begun adopting into law — and urging paediatricians to evaluate screen use during routine checkups.

The advisory lands alongside a separate study, published this week in the journal Brain Health, that may carry the more alarming finding. Researchers introduced the concept of the "criticome" — the idea that experiences from birth through young adulthood actively shape who we become as adults. The study warned that heavy screen use may be crowding out the very activities that make healthy development happen: playing with other children, exploring outdoors, learning music, art and sports.

What worried the researchers most was the irreversibility. Unlike a bad grade that can be recovered, certain developmental windows, once closed, do not reopen. Some of the cognitive, social and emotional gaps tied to early childhood screen overuse may be permanent.

## The Numbers Behind the Warning

The evidence cited across both the advisory and supporting research is extensive:

A 2025 meta-analysis in JAMA Network Open involving 335,000 participants found that each extra hour of daily screen time increases myopia risk by 21 per cent. The 2026 SCAMP study from Imperial College London found that using social media for more than three hours daily doubles the risk of depression and anxiety symptoms. Research published in Pediatrics linked smartphone ownership at age 12 to a 40 per cent higher risk of obesity and a 31 per cent higher risk of depression.

A separate study published this week in JAMA Pediatrics concluded that the earliest safe age for a child to receive a smartphone is 13 — and even at that age, poor sleep remained a significant concern. Delaying by even one year was associated with measurably better mental and physical health outcomes.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For South Asian families in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the Gulf, the advisory touches a nerve that runs deeper than screen-time limits.

Indian-American households are among the most connected in the country. The typical South Asian family is more likely to work in the technology sector, more likely to own multiple devices per household member and, by extension, more likely to normalise early device exposure as an extension of educational ambition rather than a risk factor.

The cultural context adds layers. Video calls with grandparents in India are a non-negotiable lifeline for diaspora children's linguistic and emotional connection to their heritage. Tamil, Hindi or Telugu YouTube channels sometimes serve as the only sustained exposure to a mother tongue. Restricting screen time wholesale can feel like restricting cultural transmission.

The challenge for diaspora parents is calibration, not abstinence. The Surgeon General's framework allows for intentional, structured use — it targets the passive, unsupervised scrolling and gaming that displaces developmental essentials, not a ten-minute FaceTime with a grandparent in Chennai.

## What Schools Are Doing

The institutional response is already shifting. More than a dozen US states have enacted or are advancing legislation to ban personal phones in classrooms. Florida, Virginia and Indiana have implemented statewide policies. California's governor signed a bill requiring school districts to adopt phone-free policies, effective this academic year.

Apple, at its Worldwide Developers Conference this week, previewed expanded parental controls that will let parents set tighter time-of-day restrictions on apps, control who children can communicate with and filter content more granularly.

## What Parents Can Do Now

The Brain Health researchers recommended a simple hierarchy: real-world interaction first, structured screen time second, passive scrolling never. They encouraged parents to audit their children's total daily screen hours — including school-issued devices — and to prioritise unstructured outdoor play, creative activities and face-to-face socialisation.

For diaspora families, that might mean keeping the daily video call with Nani but replacing the post-dinner YouTube session with a board game, a walk or a book.

The researchers were blunt in their conclusion: technology is a tool, but it should not be the default environment for a developing brain.

*Sources: US Surgeon General Advisory (2026); Brain Health (2026); JAMA Pediatrics (2026); JAMA Network Open (2025); Imperial College London SCAMP Study*
